newsitem.title: CANADA: Abitibi-Cons sees firmer newsprint prices.
newsitem.headline: Abitibi-Cons sees firmer newsprint prices.

text.p: James Doughan, president and chief executive of Abitibi-Consolidated Inc, said on Thursday that the North American publishing industry expects two newsprint price increases this year, including the one currently in effect.

"I think the publishing industry expects two price increases this year, including the one that's already in effect," Doughan told reporters shortly after Stone-Consolidated shareholders approved the company's C$4.1 billion merger amalgamation with Abitibi-Price.
Doughan declined to speculate on the amount of any further price increase, but added that publishers fought hard against a March 1 US$75-a-tonne hike in newsprint prices.
Doughan, who was also president and chief executive of Stone-Consoldiated before the merger, said that company's transaction prices for newsprint were US$570 a metric ton.

Doughan said he was optimistic that the newsprint market would improve during the year. One source of uncertainty, however, was Western Canada, where Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd was in contract talks with two major unions.
"I am not familiar with the details, but my understanding is that they are poles apart in what they are asking," Doughan said.
"I think there is some concern on the part of publisher and producer alike that there is also a possibility ... of a strike on the west coast," he said.
That would lead producers to continue to operate at high levels to maintain inventories, he added.
Fletcher Canada is majority owned by New Zealand's Fletcher Challenge Ltd.
In his speech to shareholders, Doughan said the newsprint industry cannot continue to operate at very high output levels because forecasts do not show a "sold-out situation."
"We think the industry should not continue flat-out production," he said.
High output levels make it more difficult to keep inventories in balance with demand, he said.
"We find this worrisome despite the fact that inventories have decreased during this (latest) period," he said.

Doughan told reporters that Roger Stone, major shareholder of Stone Container Corp, which owns 47 percent of Stone-Consolidated and would own 25 percent of Abitibi-Consolidated, has not indicated any plans to sell his stake in the the merged company in the short term.
"Roger has told me he is not interested in selling his share of Stone-Consolidated and paying the tax bill that he would have to pay on it," Doughan said. ((Reuters Montreal bureau 514-985-2434))
